title: Super sector not obligated to solve Australia’s problems: IFM
full_text:
IFM Investors says the $4.5 trillion superannuation industry will fiercely resist any move by policymakers to try to steer investments towards national interests and continue its hunt for returns overseas, arguing that fixing the federal government’s problems is not the sector’s job.
Owned by a group of local industry superannuation funds and global pension providers, IFM is one of the country’s largest global investors with 17 offices around the world managing a portfolio of assets worth close to $300 billion.
It has led the sector’s push into global markets, organising summits in the United States and Europe – and is in Canada this week to spruik the investment prowess of big super.
IFM global external relations head David Whiteley said superannuation was undoubtedly part of Australia’s diplomatic strategy, as funds reach the limit of what they can invest in locally and instead invest overseas to maintain competitive returns for members.
However, he dismissed the idea that funds should be directed to resolve the government’s problems.
“It is not the job of industry super funds to resolve the economic issues that Australia has,” Whiteley said. “Australian super funds can afford to be selective with their investments to get the best returns for their members.”
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said last month super funds could be used “as a national asset that can be used more appropriately” to drive member returns and boost areas of national interest.
“CEOs will resist that strongly,” Whiteley said.
He cautioned that there had not yet been any direct suggestions from the government, primarily from Treasurer Jim Chalmers, that the industry would be steered towards investing in areas such as housing or the energy transition.
The government has, however, floated changes to the annual superannuation performance test that are designed to make it easier for the funds to justify outlays to these sectors, despite the far weaker investment returns on offer.
Whiteley said the sector was in an advantageous position to invest globally by leveraging Australia’s reputation on the world stage.
“With the size and growth of the Australian super system, there is a need to continue to diversify globally,” he said. “Australian super funds can afford to be selective with their investments to get better returns for their members.”
Association of Super Funds of Australia chief executive Mary Delahunty said competition for superannuation investment globally was becoming more intense and local policymakers should not feel they are owed investment from the sector.
“Foreign governments are working hard to attract Australian capital,” she said, referencing comments from outgoing Macquarie chief executive Shemara Wikramanayake, who accused the country of being complacent about how it attracts investment and capital.
“[Those foreign governments] tend to understand Australian institutional investors need investment-ready assets that match the risk-return requirements for our members. The federal government, state governments and local governments; they need to work hard to attract investment too.”
IFM is touring Canada with its backers to scout opportunities and build relationships with the government and businesses.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney signed a memorandum of understanding with Australia when he visited this year for greater co-operation and investment between their sprawling pension funds during his visit.
Canada has the world’s second-largest pension system and Australia’s is the fourth-biggest by assets under management, with similar specialities in the infrastructure industry.
IFM has been growing its presence in Canada over the past 12 months by opening a new office in Toronto and flagging plans to invest $10 billion in the country over the next decade.
“Building relationships in different markets takes time, and they can often start with MoUs, but take some time to translate to investment,” Whiteley said. “We are raising the profile of super funds in the Canadian market.”
“This Australian pool of capital … is attractive because of our status as a reliable middle power.”
